newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition plan protests on re-vote day.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition plan protests on re-vote day.

text.p: Opposition parties, riding a tide that has produced Serbia's biggest mass protests in five years, plan more marches against a re-vote on Wednesday in local elections they say they have already won.
Belgrade's electoral commission has warned the opposition to respect the law which bans campaigning for the last two days before voting.

But the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition predicted a high turnout in cities across the country in spite of winter weather and said protests were gaining momentum as supporters realised President Slobodan Milosevic did not intend to accept his followers' unexpected defeat.
The supreme court on Tuesday rejected a Zajedno appeal to cancel Wednesday's re-vote and uphold the results of mid-November's second-round voting.

An estimated 40,000 people marched through freezing rain past the state television studios and the state-controlled newspaper Politika -- both instruments of Milosevic's power -- pelting them with eggs and abuse.
The protest's reached a peak on Monday when more than 100,000 people jammed the centre of Belgrade.
After run-off votes 10 days ago, local election commissions around the country announced opposition victories in 15 of the country's 18 largest towns and cities including Belgrade.
But the commissions -- all under the control of Milosevic's Socialists -- then annulled almost all the wins, citing unspecified irregularities, and called another round of voting for Wednesday.
The United States, which sees Milosevic as a key guarantor of the agreement that ended fighting in Bosnia last year, condemned the election annulments on Tuesday.
The European Union postponed giving Yugoslavia preferential trade status granted to its neighbours.
Tens of thousands of people have demonstrated each day demanding acceptance of the opposition victories.
The scale of Zajedno's apparent win and subsequent public support appeared to have caught the newly formed coalition off guard.
"Yesterday we didn't know that there would be more than 100,000 people in the streets," opposition leader Zoran Djindjic told Reuters. "This is all new for us."

"I thought no one would come today because the weather is exceptionaly terrible and yesterday was a real climax. But the crowd was much more radical than Monday's -- I think they are getting frustrated," he said.
